prompt: A student surveys a random sample of $20$ classmates and finds that $6$ own a car. She wants a one-proportion $z$-interval for the proportion of all 2,000 students at the school who own a car. Which condition for the interval is NOT met?

choices.label: The sample was not selected at random.
The number of successes, $6$, is less than $10$ (Large Counts).
The sample is more than $10\%$ of the population.
The sample proportion $0.30$ is too far from $0.50$.

hint: The three conditions: Random, $10\%$ (sample $< 10\%$ of population), and Large Counts ($n\hat{p} \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 10$).

hints.text: The three conditions: Random, $10\%$ (sample $< 10\%$ of population), and Large Counts ($n\hat{p} \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 10$).

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: a random sample of 50 with 25 successes passes everything: random ✓, $50 < 200$ ✓, $25 \ge 10$ and $25 \ge 10$ ✓. Now test each condition with 20 and 6.
Random ✓. $20 < 10\%$ of 2,000 $= 200$ ✓. Successes: $6$. Failures: $14$. Are both at least 10?
Only $6$ successes — fewer than 10 — so Large Counts fails. Choice B.

explanation: Random condition: the prompt says the sample is random, so A is not the problem.
$10\%$ condition: $20 \le 0.10 \times 2000 = 200$, fine, so C is not it. D is not a real condition — $\hat{p}$ can be anything.
Large Counts: $n\hat{p} = 6 < 10$. With so few successes the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is not close to normal, so the $z$-interval is not appropriate. B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why it matters
steps: The $z$-interval borrows the normal curve to set its margin of error.
With only 6 successes, the possible values of $\hat{p}$ are lumpy and skewed, so the normal curve gives a misleading margin.
She needs a bigger sample — at least 34 students at this rate — before the normal-based interval is trustworthy.
